identification.summary: UAT-9921 is an uncategorized threat actor cluster that Cisco Talos named in February 2026 after observing it deploy the VoidLink malware framework against victims in the technology sector and, to a lesser extent, financial services [S1][S2]. VoidLink was first publicly documented by Check Point Research in January 2026 as a modular, cloud-focused Linux framework written in Zig [S4][S5]. Talos assesses that the actor appears to have been active since at least 2019, not necessarily using VoidLink for that whole period [S2][S3].
identification.firstObserved: Talos: appears active since at least 2019 [S2]. Talos is aware of VoidLink-related victims from September (read by The Hacker News as September 2025) through January 2026 [S2].
identification.notes: UAT-designations are Talos's temporary labels for clusters not yet tied to a known group. Talos assesses the actor has knowledge of Chinese language based on framework language, code comments and code planning done in an AI-enabled IDE [S2][S3]. Check Point's report and Talos's report differ in timeline: Talos says the documents Check Point examined reflected VoidLink version 2.0 while the actor it tracked was still on version 1.0 [S2]. No Microsoft name or MITRE group ID is known for this cluster.

attribution.confidence: Talos makes language-based and timeline assessments (Chinese-language knowledge; activity since at least 2019 as a hedged assessment) but no state-sponsor attribution is stated in the sources gathered [S2][S3]. Check Point described the samples as appearing to originate from a Chinese-affiliated development environment and said the developers' exact affiliation remained unclear [S7]. Coverage that calls the activity state-affiliated is press speculation, not a Check Point finding [S7].
attribution.basis: Chinese-language artifacts in framework and code comments (Talos) [S2][S3]; Chinese-affiliated development environment (Check Point, as reported) [S7]. Talos also stated it cannot discount that the activity is part of red-team exercises [S2].

targeting.notes: Talos says the actor appears to focus on the technology sector but has also hit financial services; it judged that VoidLink's cloud-aware design and scanning of entire Class C networks indicate no specific targeting [S2][S3]. Victim countries are not given in the sources gathered.

capabilities.summary: Talos assesses with high confidence that UAT-9921 gains initial access with pre-obtained credentials or by exploiting Java serialization vulnerabilities, with Apache Dubbo named as an example; possible malicious-document delivery was suspected but no samples were obtained [S2]. After compromise the actor deploys a SOCKS server on victim servers, which FSCAN uses for internal reconnaissance [S2][S3]. VoidLink is a Zig-based modular framework with in-memory plugins (counts reported as over 30 or 37), cloud-provider detection (AWS, GCP, Azure, Alibaba, Tencent), container and Kubernetes awareness, and rootkit options chosen by kernel (LD_PRELOAD, loadable kernel module, eBPF) [S4][S8][S9]. It supports HTTP/HTTPS, ICMP and DNS tunneling C2, and reports describe experimental peer-to-peer or mesh routing [S8][S9]. Talos reports clear indications of Windows implants able to load plugins [S3]. Check Point assessed development was largely AI-driven and likely by a single developer, with a first functional implant in under a week; Talos says development appears AI-supported but operations do not rely on AI [S3][S4][S6].

campaigns.name: Earliest activity (hedged assessment)
campaigns.summary: Talos assesses UAT-9921 has been active since at least 2019, possibly with other tooling than VoidLink.

campaigns.name: Earliest known VoidLink-related victims
campaigns.summary: Talos is aware of VoidLink victims dating back to September (The Hacker News reads this as 2025), continuing through January 2026, mainly technology with some financial services.

campaigns.name: Check Point obtains VoidLink samples
campaigns.summary: Check Point reportedly found VoidLink samples in December 2025, appearing to be in-progress builds with debug artifacts; no in-the-wild infections had been observed at publication.

campaigns.name: Check Point publishes VoidLink analysis
campaigns.summary: Check Point publicly describes the Zig-based cloud-focused Linux framework, then follows with analysis that it was largely AI-built by one developer.

campaigns.name: Talos names UAT-9921
campaigns.summary: Talos publishes a report linking active VoidLink use to a new actor, UAT-9921, with credential or Java deserialization access, SOCKS plus FSCAN reconnaissance, and technology and finance victims.

diamond.adversary: Unnamed cluster tracked by Talos as UAT-9921; Chinese-language knowledge assessed; sponsor unknown [S2][S3].
diamond.capability: VoidLink modular framework, SOCKS server, FSCAN scanning, credential use and Java serialization exploitation such as Apache Dubbo [S2][S3][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised victim servers used as SOCKS hosts; VoidLink C2 over HTTP/HTTPS, ICMP and DNS with reported mesh options [S2][S8][S9]. Specific C2 infrastructure is not in the sources gathered.
diamond.victim: Technology and financial services organizations; broad Class C scanning suggests no specific targeting [S2][S3].
diamond.technology: Linux servers and cloud workloads (AWS, GCP, Azure, Alibaba, Tencent), containers and Kubernetes, and internet-facing Java services such as Apache Dubbo [S2][S4][S8].

gaps: The Talos primary report, Check Point primary report and Isovalent post could not be opened (fetch tool had no network access); facts rest on search-result excerpts and secondary coverage, so wording should be verified against [S1] and [S4].
No state-sponsor, MSS/PLA link or government attribution is stated in the sources; Talos itself notes the activity could be red-team exercises.

The imported summary claims a ZigLang implant with a GoLang backend, P2P mesh C2, eBPF persistence, and targeting of IoT and critical infrastructure; the sources gathered support Zig, reported mesh options and eBPF rootkit options, but not Go, IoT or critical-infrastructure targeting.
Victim names, countries and counts are not public in the sources gathered; whether the activity predating 2025 used other malware is unknown.

Differences between Check Point (VoidLink v2.0, no in-the-wild infections, possible commercial product) and Talos (v1.0, active victims) are not fully reconciled; the relationship between the VoidLink developer and the UAT-9921 operators is unclear.
Windows implant capability is described as clear indications by one outlet and as possible by others.
Microsoft name, MITRE group ID and overlap with named clusters are unknown.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is Linux servers and cloud workloads in technology and finance, especially internet-facing Java services and cloud metadata and credential stores [S2][S4]. STEP 2: The actor is opportunistic, scanning whole Class C networks, so exposure rather than mission relevance drives targeting; DoD-adjacent contractors hosting Java/Dubbo or cloud Linux workloads are plausible victims [S2][S3]. STEP 3: Observed pattern is stolen credentials or Java deserialization, then SOCKS server and FSCAN reconnaissance, then VoidLink with plugins and rootkit-based concealment [S2][S4]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued opportunistic access to technology and finance servers. MDCOA, which is speculative, is use of the stealthy framework against cloud environments supporting defense contractors for long-term access. Candidate indicators: unexpected SOCKS listeners, FSCAN-style sweeps of Class C ranges, LD_PRELOAD changes, unexpected kernel modules or eBPF programs, and access to the cloud metadata service [S2][S8][S9].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track Talos and Check Point updates, since the framework and actor timelines are not yet reconciled [S2][S7]. (2) Authorities: hunting on cloud and contractor-hosted systems requires owner or DIB-program coordination. (3) Mission assurance: rootkit-capable implants undermine host-based telemetry, so rely on network and cloud-log visibility and credential hygiene for Java-service hosts [S4][S9]. (4) Coordination: share indicators through established DC3/DIB channels and treat attribution to a state as unconfirmed.
